passages.happening:
John, who has just eaten the scroll and been told to prophesy, is handed a tool: “Then I was given a measuring rod like a staff and was told, ‘Go and measure the temple of God and the altar, and count the number of worshipers there’” (verse 1).

But not all of it: “But exclude the courtyard outside the temple. Do not measure it, because it has been given over to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for 42 months” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
The interlude that began in chapter 10 goes on. John has been told to prophesy. Now he sees what faithful witness looks like in a hostile world.

In the prophets, measuring something was a sign that it belonged to God and was under his protection. The Greek word is metreō. The inner part of the temple, its altar and its worshippers are measured: they are kept. The outer court is left out: it is open to trampling. Many readers take the picture this way. God's people are kept safe in their relationship with him, even while they are outwardly trampled.

‘42 months’ is three and a half years, the same period as ‘1,260 days’ in the next verse. The figure comes from Daniel's ‘a time, times, and half a time’. That language grew out of the persecution of the Jewish people by the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, who defiled the temple in Jerusalem in 167 BC. It was cleansed and dedicated again in 164 BC, which is the origin of Hanukkah. Three and a half, half of seven, became a standard figure for a time of distress that is real but cut short, limited by God. The same period comes again in chapters 12 and 13.
passages.ot:
Measuring is the prophets' sign. Ezekiel saw a man “with a linen cord and a measuring rod in his hand” (Ezekiel 40:3), who measured a temple still to come. Zechariah saw “a man with a measuring line in his hand”, going “To measure Jerusalem” (Zechariah 2:1-2), as a sign that God would live there.

The period of trouble is Daniel's: “the saints will be given into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time” (Daniel 7:25).

And Jesus warned that “Jerusalem will be trodden down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled” (Luke 21:24).
passages.hard:
What is this temple? Is it the temple in Jerusalem, a temple still to come, or something else?

Christians read it in the four ways the book page sets out, and these notes do not choose. Some preterists take it as the real temple in Jerusalem before the Romans destroyed it in AD 70, and the 42 months as the time of the Jewish war. That reading fits best if the book was written before AD 70; if it was written about AD 95, the temple had been gone for a generation, and most take the picture as symbolic. Futurists often expect a temple in Jerusalem in a final period of three and a half years. Historicists have read the measuring as part of their map of the church's history. Idealists and many others read the temple as the people of God, as Paul does: “Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

These notes tie this picture to no nation, government, building or event of our own day.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you to be ‘measured’, known and kept by God, even when life feels trampled. Ask whether you think of your church as a temple where God lives. And ask how you would hold your view of this passage humbly, beside Christians who read it another way.

passages.happening:
The voice goes on: “And I will empower my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth” (verse 3).

John is told who they are: “These witnesses are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth” (verse 4).

He sees their power. Fire comes from their mouths to devour anyone who wants to harm them (verse 5). “These witnesses have power to shut the sky so that no rain will fall during the days of their prophecy, and power to turn the waters into blood and to strike the earth with every kind of plague as often as they wish” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The witnesses wear sackcloth, the rough cloth of mourning and repentance. Their message is a call to turn back to God.

They are ‘two’ because the Law required two witnesses to establish a matter. And they are ‘the two olive trees and the two lampstands’. That picture comes from Zechariah, where two olive trees supply oil to a lampstand and stand for two anointed leaders, Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor. And in Revelation, lampstands are the image for churches (1:20).

Their powers are those of two great prophets. Elijah shut the sky so that no rain fell, and called down fire. Moses turned the water of the Nile into blood and brought plagues on Egypt. The witnesses carry the authority of the Law and the Prophets together.

The Greek word for witness, martus, means one who testifies to what they know. Revelation calls Jesus ‘the faithful witness’ (1:5). By the second century the word was coming to mean a martyr, because witness to Christ so often led to death. This chapter shows why.

What of the fire from their mouths? Revelation never asks God's people to take up arms. Christ's own sword comes from his mouth: it is his word. Here too the witnesses' power is the power of what they speak.
passages.ot:
The olive trees are Zechariah's: “There are also two olive trees beside it” (Zechariah 4:3). “These are the two anointed ones who are standing beside the Lord of all the earth” (Zechariah 4:14).

Elijah shut the sky: “there will be neither dew nor rain in these years except at my word!” (1 Kings 17:1). Jesus said that in Elijah's time “the sky was shut for three and a half years” (Luke 4:25). Elijah called down fire: “And fire came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men” (2 Kings 1:10).

Moses turned the water to blood: “all the water was turned to blood” (Exodus 7:20). And the Law asked for two witnesses: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15).
passages.hard:
Who are the two witnesses?

Christians read them in several ways, and these notes do not choose. Some preterists take them as Christian leaders of the first century; some suggest Peter and Paul, who by tradition were both put to death in Rome in the 60s. Futurists often expect two real prophets in a final period of three and a half years. Some early church writers named them as Enoch and Elijah, who in Scripture did not die; others expect Moses and Elijah, who appeared with Jesus at the Transfiguration. Historicists have matched the witnesses with faithful groups through the church's history. Idealists and many others read the two witnesses as the witnessing church itself, pointing out that they are called lampstands, the book's image for churches, and that they are two because the Law required two witnesses.

These are questions on which faithful readers differ. These notes name no person, church or group of our own day as the two witnesses. On every reading, the chapter's direction is the same: faithful witness costs, and God vindicates.
passages.asks: Ask what it would mean for your life to be a witness, testifying to what you know of Christ. Ask whether your words carry the weight of God's word, or only your own opinions. And ask what ‘sackcloth’ might look like for a church today: grief over its own sins as well as the world's.

passages.happening:
When their testimony is finished, John sees them overcome: “the beast that comes up from the Abyss will wage war with them, and will overpower and kill them” (verse 7).

“Their bodies will lie in the street of the great city—figuratively called Sodom and Egypt—where their Lord was also crucified” (verse 8). For three and a half days people from every nation look at their bodies and refuse to let them be buried (verse 9).

“And those who dwell on the earth will gloat over them, and will celebrate and send one another gifts, because these two prophets had tormented them” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
This is the first mention of ‘the beast’, who will come into full view in chapter 13. It rises from the Abyss, the bottomless deep of chapter 9.

Notice the timing: ‘When the two witnesses have finished their testimony’. They are not killed a moment before their work is done. God sets the limit even here.

To leave bodies unburied was among the deepest dishonours in the ancient world. And the world keeps holiday over their deaths. Sending gifts to one another was a way of celebrating a festival, as at Purim in the book of Esther. The truth these prophets told had ‘tormented’ the people who heard it. Now people are glad to be rid of them.

‘The great city’ is called, figuratively, ‘Sodom and Egypt’. Sodom was the city of proud wickedness; Egypt was the land of slavery and of Pharaoh, who opposed God's people. The names describe a city's character. And it is the city ‘where their Lord was also crucified’. Which city is meant is discussed below.

The story of the witnesses follows the story of Jesus. They testify, they are killed in the city where their Lord died, and their deaths are celebrated. It tells the church that faithful witness will walk the same road its Lord walked.
passages.ot:
The unburied dead are the psalm's lament: “They have given the corpses of Your servants as food to the birds of the air” and “there is no one to bury the dead” (Psalm 79:2-3).

And the exchange of gifts recalls Purim, when the Jews kept days “of feasting and joy, of sending gifts to one another and to the poor” (Esther 9:22). Here, terribly, the same festive custom marks the death of God's prophets.
passages.hard:
What is ‘the great city’, ‘where their Lord was also crucified’?

Readers take it in more than one way, and these notes do not choose. Some take it as Jerusalem, where Jesus was crucified. Others point out that Revelation elsewhere calls Babylon ‘the great city’ (16:19; 18:10), and read it as a picture of the whole world set against God, given the names Sodom and Egypt to show its character. On this reading, Christ is crucified wherever his witnesses are rejected.

One thing must be said plainly. If the city is Jerusalem, the verse is still no word against the Jewish people. Jesus, his first disciples and the crowds who welcomed him were Jews, and a Roman governor gave the order for his death. For centuries many Christians used scenes like this to justify contempt and violence against Jews. That reading is false. This site rejects it, and the note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why.

And the passage honours the witnesses without praising death. They did not seek it. They were killed by others for telling the truth, and God answers that wrong in the next verses.

Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask why people so often resent those who tell them the truth. Ask whether you have ever been glad to see a hard voice silenced. And ask how you can stand with Christians today who are mocked or harmed for their witness.

passages.happening:
Then everything turns: “But after the three and a half days, the breath of life from God entered the two witnesses, and they stood on their feet, and great fear fell upon those who saw them” (verse 11).

The witnesses hear a voice from heaven: “Come up here.” “And they went up to heaven in a cloud as their enemies watched them” (verse 12).

“And in that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city collapsed. Seven thousand were killed in the quake, and the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven” (verse 13). “The second woe has passed. Behold, the third woe is coming shortly” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The witnesses' story is a short gospel: ministry, rejection, death in the city where their Lord was crucified, a public display, then resurrection and ascension in a cloud while their enemies watch. Jesus was taken up in a cloud too. What happened to the Lord happens to his witnesses. Death is not the end of the faithful.

‘Come up here’ is the same call John heard at the door of heaven in 4:1.

And then something new happens. After the plagues of the trumpets, people ‘did not repent’ (9:20-21). After the witness, death and rising of God's prophets, ‘the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven’. Many interpreters see here the book's answer to chapter 9. Judgments alone did not turn people. Faithful witness, through death and resurrection, does.

The numbers are measured: a tenth of the city falls, seven thousand die, and the rest, the great majority, give glory to God. In earlier judgments, a fourth and then a third were struck. Here most are spared, and they turn.
passages.ot:
The breath of life is Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones: “So I prophesied as He had commanded me, and the breath entered them, and they came to life and stood on their feet—a vast army” (Ezekiel 37:10).

And they go up in a cloud, as Jesus did: “they watched as He was taken up, and a cloud hid Him from their sight” (Acts 1:9).
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that God's last word over his faithful people is not death but ‘Come up here’. Ask what kind of witness actually turns hearts, in your experience. And ask whether you are more ready to see people judged or to see them give glory to God.

passages.t: The seventh trumpet: the kingdom has come
passages.happening:
At last the seventh angel blows his trumpet, and John hears loud voices in heaven: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever” (verse 15).

The twenty-four elders fall on their faces and worship God, saying: “We give thanks to You, O Lord God Almighty, the One who is and who was, because You have taken Your great power and have begun to reign” (verses 16-17). “The nations were enraged, and Your wrath has come. The time has come to judge the dead and to reward Your servants the prophets, as well as the saints and those who fear Your name, both small and great— and to destroy those who destroy the earth” (verse 18).

“Then the temple of God in heaven was opened, and the ark of His covenant appeared in His temple. And there were flashes of lightning, and rumblings, and peals of thunder, and an earthquake, and a great hailstorm” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The angel in chapter 10 swore there would be no more delay. Now the seventh trumpet sounds, and heaven sings the end of the story before the book has told it.

‘The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ.’ The word kingdom, basileia, is singular. The kingdoms of this world are not only defeated; they are taken over. There is one kingdom, with one rightful king. ‘His Christ’ means his Messiah, his anointed king. This line, with 19:6 and 16, is among the texts Handel set in the Hallelujah chorus of Messiah in 1742.

Listen to God's name in the elders' song. In 1:8 and 4:8 he is the one ‘who was and is and is to come’. Here he is ‘the One who is and who was’. The words ‘is to come’ are gone, because in the vision he has come, and he has begun to reign.

The song names what that reign brings. It judges the dead. It rewards God's servants, ‘both small and great’, the famous and the unknown alike. And it destroys ‘those who destroy the earth’. God's judgment falls on those who ruin what he made.

Then the temple in heaven opens, and the ark of the covenant is seen. The ark was the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the Law, the footstool of God's throne in Israel's sanctuary. It vanished when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. Seeing it in heaven tells the churches that God's covenant has never been lost. And the storm signs that closed the seals come again, with hail added. Another ending is reached.
passages.ot:
The joining of God and his anointed king is Psalm 2: “The kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together, against the LORD and against His Anointed One” (Psalm 2:2). God answers: “I have installed My King on Zion, upon My holy mountain” (Psalm 2:6).

The everlasting kingdom is Daniel's: “His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed” (Daniel 7:14).

And Jeremiah foresaw a day when the lost ark would not be missed: “It will never come to mind, and no one will remember it or miss it, nor will another one be made” (Jeremiah 3:16). In Revelation, God's covenant presence is seen in heaven itself.
passages.asks: Ask how it might change your week to live as though God's reign is already announced. Ask what it means to you that God rewards ‘both small and great’. And ask what you are doing with the part of his earth that has been put in your care.
